systemctl.documentation:
Introspect and control the state of the systemd system and service manager.
Manages units (services, mount points, sockets, timers), monitors system state,
and controls boot and shutdown behavior. Operates on the system manager by
default; use `--user` to target the per-user service manager.

commands.name: add-requires
commands.description: Add 'Requires' dependency for the target on specified one or more units
commands.documentation:
Add "Requires=" dependencies for the specified TARGET to one or more units.
This command honors --system, --user, --runtime and --global in the same
way as enable.

commands.name: add-wants
commands.description: Add 'Wants' dependency for the target on specified one or more units
commands.documentation:
Add "Wants=" dependencies for the specified TARGET to one or more units.
This command honors --system, --user, --runtime and --global in the same
way as enable.

commands.name: bind
commands.description: Bind-mount a path from the host into a unit's namespace
commands.documentation:
Bind-mount a file or directory from the host into the specified unit's
mount namespace. The first path argument is the source on the host, the
second is the destination in the unit's namespace (omitted if same as
source). Use `--read-only` for a read-only bind mount, `--mkdir` to
create the destination first. Note this is only supported for units that
run within a mount namespace (e.g., with RootImage=, PrivateMounts=).
The bind mount is ephemeral and is undone when the unit process exits.

commands.name: cancel
commands.description: Cancel all, one, or more jobs
commands.documentation:
Cancel one or more jobs specified on the command line by their
numeric job IDs. If no job ID is specified, cancel all pending jobs.

commands.name: cat
commands.description: Show files and drop-ins of specified units
commands.documentation:
Show backing files of one or more units. Prints the "fragment" and
"drop-ins" (source files) of units. Each file is preceded by a comment
which includes the file name. Note that this shows the contents of the
backing files on disk, which might not match the system manager's
understanding if unit files were updated and daemon-reload was not run.

commands.name: clean
commands.description: Clean runtime, cache, state, logs or configuration of unit
commands.documentation:
Remove the configuration, state, cache, logs, runtime, or file descriptor
store data of the specified units. Use `--what=` to select which kind of
resource to remove. For service units, this removes directories configured
with ConfigurationDirectory=, StateDirectory=, CacheDirectory=, LogsDirectory=
and RuntimeDirectory=. For timer units with Persistent=, use `--what=state`
to clear persistent timestamp data. If `--what=` is not specified, cache
and runtime data as well as the file descriptor store are removed.

commands.name: daemon-reexec
commands.description: Reexecute systemd manager
commands.documentation:
Reexecute the systemd manager. This will serialize the manager state,
reexecute the process and deserialize the state again. This command is
of little use except for debugging and package upgrades. Sometimes it
might be helpful as a heavy-weight daemon-reload.

commands.name: daemon-reload
commands.description: Reload systemd manager configuration
commands.documentation:
Reload the systemd manager configuration. This will rerun all generators,
reload all unit files, and recreate the entire dependency tree. While
reloading, all sockets systemd listens on behalf of user configuration
will stay accessible. This command should not be confused with the reload
command which reloads service-specific configuration.

commands.name: default
commands.description: Enter system default mode
commands.documentation:
Enter default mode. This is equivalent to `systemctl isolate default.target`.
This operation is blocking by default; use `--no-block` for asynchronous
behavior. This is typically the normal boot target.

commands.name: disable
commands.description: Disable one or more unit files
commands.documentation:
Disable one or more units. This removes all symlinks to the unit files
from the unit configuration directory, undoing any changes made by enable
or link. Note that this removes all symlinks to matching unit files,
including manually created symlinks, not just those created by enable.
This command also disables all units listed in the Also= setting of any
of the unit files being operated on. This command does not implicitly
stop the units being disabled; use `--now` to also stop them.

commands.name: edit
commands.description: Edit one or more unit files
commands.documentation:
Edit or replace a drop-in snippet or the main unit file to extend or
override the definition of the specified unit. If `--full` is specified,
a replacement for the main unit file will be created. Otherwise, a
drop-in file will be created. Use `--drop-in=` to specify a drop-in file
name instead of the default override.conf. Use `--force` to edit a
nonexistent unit or create a drop-in for one. Use `--stdin` to read new
contents from standard input.

commands.name: emergency
commands.description: Enter system emergency mode
commands.documentation:
Enter emergency mode. This is equivalent to `systemctl isolate emergency.target`.
This operation is blocking by default; use `--no-block` for asynchronous
behavior. In emergency mode, only a minimal set of services is started
and users are given a recovery shell with minimal resources available.

commands.name: enable
commands.description: Enable one or more unit files
commands.documentation:
Enable one or more units or unit instances. This creates symlinks as
encoded in the [Install] sections of the indicated unit files. After
the symlinks have been created, the system manager configuration is
reloaded. Note that this does not start any of the units being enabled;
use `--now` to also start them. Enabling and starting units is orthogonal:
enabling hooks the unit into suggested places (e.g. boot), while starting
actually spawns the daemon process. Using enable on masked units is not
supported and results in an error.

commands.name: enqueue-marked
commands.description: Enqueue jobs for all marked units
commands.documentation:
Enqueue start/stop/restart/reload jobs for all units that have the
respective "needs-*" markers set. When a unit marked for reload does
not support reload, restart will be queued. Those properties can be
set using set-property Markers=.... Unless --no-block is used,
systemctl will wait for the queued jobs to finish.

commands.name: exit
commands.description: Request user instance or container exit
commands.documentation:
Request user instance or container exit. With no arguments, this
terminates the current user manager (for --user) or the container's
PID 1. Takes an optional exit code and/or status string argument.

commands.name: freeze
commands.description: Freeze execution of unit processes
commands.documentation:
Freeze one or more units using cgroup freezer. Freezing causes all
processes contained within the unit's cgroup to be suspended; they
will not be scheduled to run on CPU until thawed. Note that this
command is supported only on systems using unified cgroup hierarchy.
Units are automatically thawed just before executing a job against
them (e.g. before stopping).

commands.name: get-default
commands.description: Get the name of the default target
commands.documentation:
Return the name of the default target to boot into. This returns the
target unit name that default.target is aliased (symlinked) to.

commands.name: halt
commands.description: Shut down and halt the system
commands.documentation:
Shut down and halt the system. This is mostly equivalent to
`systemctl start halt.target --Job-mode=replace-irreversibly --no-block`,
but also prints a wall message to all users. Note that this will simply
halt the OS kernel after shutting down, leaving the hardware powered on.
Use poweroff for powering off the system. If combined with `--force`,
shutdown of all running services is skipped and all processes are killed
immediately. If `--force` is specified twice, the operation is executed
without terminating any processes or unmounting any file systems.

commands.name: help
commands.description: Show manual for one or more units
commands.documentation:
Show manual pages for one or more units, if available. If a PID is
given, the manual pages for the unit the process belongs to are shown.

commands.name: hibernate
commands.description: Hibernate the system
commands.documentation:
Hibernate the system. This will trigger a system hibernate state where
system memory is written to disk and the system is powered off. The
system will resume from disk once powered on.

commands.name: hybrid-sleep
commands.description: Hibernate and suspend the system
commands.documentation:
Hibernate and suspend the system. This combines hibernation with
suspend functionality - system state is saved to disk but memory
remains powered, allowing faster wake if battery is sufficient.

commands.name: import-environment
commands.description: Import all or some environment variables
commands.documentation:
Import all, one or more environment variables set on the client into
the systemd manager environment block. If a list of variable names is
passed, client-side values are imported. If no arguments are passed,
the entire environment block inherited by the systemctl process is
imported (deprecated as shell variables often only make sense locally).

commands.name: is-active
commands.description: Check whether units are active
commands.documentation:
Check whether any of the specified units are active (i.e. running).
Returns exit code 0 if at least one is active, non-zero otherwise.
Unless `--quiet` is specified, this also prints the current unit state
to standard output.

commands.name: is-enabled
commands.description: Check whether unit files are enabled
commands.documentation:
Check whether any of the specified unit files are enabled. Returns
exit code 0 if at least one is enabled, non-zero otherwise. Prints
the current enable status: enabled, enabled-runtime, linked,
linked-runtime, alias, masked, masked-runtime, static, indirect,
disabled, generated, transient, bad, or not-found.

commands.name: is-failed
commands.description: Check whether units are failed
commands.documentation:
Check whether any of the specified units is in the "failed" state.
If no unit is specified, check whether there are any failed units or
ordering cycles (which corresponds to the "degraded" state returned
by is-system-running). Returns exit code 0 if at least one has failed.
Unless `--quiet` is specified, also prints the current unit state.

commands.name: is-system-running
commands.description: Check whether system is fully running
commands.documentation:
Checks whether the system is operational. Returns success (exit code 0)
when the system is fully up and running, specifically not in startup,
shutdown or maintenance mode, and with no failed services. The current
state is printed to standard output: initializing, starting, running,
degraded, maintenance, stopping, offline, or unknown. Use `--wait` to
wait until boot is completed before returning.

commands.name: isolate
commands.description: Start one unit and stop all others
commands.documentation:
Start the unit specified on the command line and its dependencies and
stop all others, unless they have IgnoreOnIsolate=yes. If a unit name
with no extension is given, an extension of ".target" will be assumed.
This command is dangerous as it will immediately stop processes that
are not enabled in the new target, possibly including the graphical
environment or terminal you are currently using.

commands.name: kexec
commands.description: Shut down and reboot the system with kexec
commands.documentation:
Shut down and reboot the system via kexec. This will load a kexec kernel
if one was not loaded yet, or fail. A kernel may be loaded earlier by a
separate step using `kexec --load`. The `--force` can be used to continue
without a kexec kernel, i.e. to perform a normal reboot. Uses UEFI boot
loader specification to find and load the default boot entry.

commands.name: kill
commands.description: Send signal to processes of a unit
commands.documentation:
Send a UNIX process signal to one or more processes of the unit.
Use `--kill-whom=` to select which process to send the signal to:
main (only the main process), control (only the control process),
or all (all processes in the unit). Use `--signal=` to select the
signal to send (e.g. SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGHUP). Combine with
`--kill-value=` to enqueue a POSIX Realtime Signal with an associated
value.

commands.name: link
commands.description: Link one or more units files into the search path
commands.documentation:
Link a unit file that is not in the unit file search path into the
search path. This command expects an absolute path to a unit file.
The file system where the linked unit files are located must be
accessible when systemd is started (e.g. not under /home/ or /var/
unless those are on the root file system).

commands.name: list-automounts
commands.description: List automount units currently in memory, ordered by path
commands.documentation:
List automount units currently in memory, ordered by mount path.
If one or more PATTERNs are specified, only automount units matching
one of them are shown. Also see --show-types, --all, and --state=.

commands.name: list-dependencies
commands.description: Recursively show units which are required or wanted
commands.documentation:
Show units required and wanted by the specified units, recursively
following Requires=, Requisite=, Wants=, ConsistsOf=, BindsTo=, and
Upholds= dependencies. If no units are specified, default.target is
implied. Use `--reverse`, `--after`, `--before` to change what types
of dependencies are shown. Note that this only lists units currently
loaded into memory.

commands.name: list-jobs
commands.description: List jobs
commands.documentation:
List jobs that are in progress. If one or more PATTERNs are specified,
only jobs for units matching one of them are shown. When combined with
`--after` or `--before`, the list is augmented with information on
which other job each job is waiting for, and which other jobs are
waiting for it.

commands.name: list-machines
commands.description: List local containers and host
commands.documentation:
List the host and all running local containers with their state.
If one or more PATTERNs are specified, only containers matching one
of them are shown.

commands.name: list-paths
commands.description: List path units currently in memory, ordered by path
commands.documentation:
List path units currently in memory, ordered by path. If one or more
PATTERNs are specified, only path units matching one of them are shown.
Also see --show-types, --all, and --state=.

commands.name: list-sockets
commands.description: List socket units currently in memory, ordered by address
commands.documentation:
List socket units currently in memory, ordered by listening address.
Shows LISTEN (address being listened on), UNIT (socket unit name), and
ACTIVATES (service activated by the socket). Note that because addresses
might contain spaces, this output is not suitable for programmatic
consumption.

commands.name: list-timers
commands.description: List timer units currently in memory, ordered by next elapse
commands.documentation:
List timer units currently in memory, ordered by the time they elapse
next. Shows NEXT (next time the timer will run), LEFT (how long till
next run), LAST (last time the timer ran), PASSED (time since last run),
UNIT (name of the timer), and ACTIVATES (name of the service the timer
activates).

commands.name: list-unit-files
commands.description: List installed unit files
commands.documentation:
List unit files installed on the system, in combination with their
enablement state (as reported by is-enabled). Unlike list-units, this
command lists template units in addition to explicitly instantiated
units.

commands.name: list-units
commands.description: List units currently in memory
commands.documentation:
List units that systemd currently has in memory. This includes units
that are referenced directly or through a dependency, units pinned by
applications programmatically, or units that were active in the past
and have failed. By default, only units which are active, have pending
jobs, or have failed are shown; use `--all` to see loaded but inactive
units too. Use `--type=` and `--state=` to filter by unit type and state.

commands.name: log-level
commands.description: Get/set logging threshold for manager
commands.documentation:
If no argument is given, print the current log level of the manager.
If an optional argument LEVEL is provided, change the current log
level to LEVEL. Accepts values: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning,
notice, info, debug (or numeric values 0-7).

commands.name: log-target
commands.description: Get/set logging target for manager
commands.documentation:
If no argument is given, print the current log target of the manager.
If an optional argument TARGET is provided, change the current log
target to TARGET. Accepts values: console, kmsg, journal, syslog,
null, or auto (auto is equivalent to console if invoked interactively,
otherwise journal or syslog).

commands.name: mask
commands.description: Mask one or more units
commands.documentation:
Mask one or more units, linking them to /dev/null and making it
impossible to start them. This is a stronger version of disable, as it
prohibits all kinds of activation including enablement and manual
activation. Use `--runtime` to mask temporarily until the next reboot.
Use `--now` to ensure the units are also stopped. Note that this creates
a symlink under the unit's name in /etc/systemd/system/ (or /run/systemd/system/
if --runtime is specified). Using mask on units created locally typically
does not work since those are placed precisely in those directories.

commands.name: mount-image
commands.description: Mount an image from the host into a unit's namespace
commands.documentation:
Mount an image from the host into the specified unit's mount namespace.
The first path argument is the source image on the host, the second is
the destination directory in the unit's mount namespace. An optional
third argument specifies a colon-separated tuple of partition name and
mount options (format: partitionName:mountOptions). Use `--read-only`
for a read-only mount, `--mkdir` to create the destination first.
This is only supported for units that run within a mount namespace.

commands.name: poweroff
commands.description: Shut down and power-off the system
commands.documentation:
Shut down and power-off the system. This is mostly equivalent to
`systemctl start poweroff.target --Job-mode=replace-irreversibly --no-block`,
but also prints a wall message to all users. This command is asynchronous;
it will return after the power-off operation is enqueued without waiting
for it to complete.

commands.name: preset-all
commands.description: Enable/disable all unit files based on preset configuration
commands.documentation:
Reset all installed unit files to the defaults configured in the
preset policy files. Use `--preset-mode=` to control whether units
shall be enabled and disabled, or only enabled, or only disabled.

commands.name: preset
commands.description: Enable/disable one or more unit files based on preset configuration
commands.documentation:
Reset the enable/disable status of one or more unit files to the defaults
configured in the preset policy files. This has the same effect as disable
or enable depending on how the unit is listed in the preset files. Use
`--preset-mode=` to control whether units shall be enabled and disabled,
or only enabled, or only disabled. UNIT must be the real unit name; any
alias names are ignored silently.

commands.name: reboot
commands.description: Shut down and reboot the system
commands.documentation:
Shut down and reboot the system. This is mostly equivalent to
`systemctl start reboot.target --job-mode=replace-irreversibly --no-block`.
Use `--reboot-argument=` to pass an optional argument to the reboot(2)
system call. Options `--boot-loader-entry=`, `--boot-loader-menu=`,
and `--firmware-setup` can be used to select what to do after reboot.
If a new kernel has been loaded via kexec --load, a kexec will be
performed instead of a reboot.

commands.name: reenable
commands.description: Reenable one or more unit files
commands.documentation:
Reenable one or more units. This is a combination of disable and enable,
useful to reset the symlinks a unit file is enabled with to the defaults
configured in its [Install] section. This command implicitly reloads the
system manager configuration after completing the operation.

commands.name: reload-or-restart
commands.description: Reload one or more units if possible, otherwise start or restart
commands.documentation:
Reload one or more units if they support it. If not, stop and then
start them instead. If the units are not running yet, they will be
started.

commands.name: reload
commands.description: Reload one or more units
commands.documentation:
Ask all units listed on the command line to reload their configuration.
Note that this reloads the service-specific configuration (e.g. Apache's
httpd.conf), not the systemd unit file. To reload systemd's configuration
of a unit, use daemon-reload instead.

commands.name: rescue
commands.description: Enter system rescue mode
commands.documentation:
Enter rescue mode. This is equivalent to `systemctl isolate rescue.target`.
This operation is blocking by default; use `--no-block` for asynchronous
behavior. In rescue mode, only the basic essential services are started
and users are given a maintenance shell.

commands.name: reset-failed
commands.description: Reset failed state for all, one, or more units
commands.documentation:
Reset the "failed" state of the specified units, or if no unit name is
passed, reset the state of all units. When a unit fails, it enters the
"failed" state and its exit code and status is recorded until the service
is stopped/re-started or reset with this command. Also resets start rate
limit counters and restart counters of service units.

commands.name: restart
commands.description: Start or restart one or more units
commands.documentation:
Stop and then start one or more units specified on the command line.
If the units are not running yet, they will be started. Note that
restarting a unit does not necessarily flush out all of the unit's
resources before it is started again. For example, the per-service
file descriptor storage (FileDescriptorStoreMax=) will remain intact
as long as the unit has a job pending.

commands.name: revert
commands.description: Revert one or more unit files to vendor version
commands.documentation:
Revert one or more unit files to their vendor versions. This removes
drop-in configuration files and any user-configured unit files that
override a matching vendor-supplied unit file. For a unit "foo.service",
it removes "foo.service.d/" directories and any persistent or runtime
unit files that override it. If a unit is masked, it is unmasked.
Effectively undoes all changes made with edit, set-property, and mask.

commands.name: service-log-level
commands.description: Get/set logging threshold for service
commands.documentation:
If no argument is given, print the current log level as reported by
the service. If an optional argument LEVEL is provided, change the
current log level of the service to LEVEL. Accepts syslog log levels
(0-7 or emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug). The
service must implement the generic org.freedesktop.LogControl1 interface.

commands.name: service-log-target
commands.description: Get/set logging target for service
commands.documentation:
If no argument is given, print the current log target as reported by
the service. If an optional argument TARGET is provided, change the
current log target to TARGET. Accepts values: console (stderr), kmsg
(kernel log), journal (systemd-journald), syslog, null, or auto.
The service must implement the generic org.freedesktop.LogControl1
interface.

commands.name: service-watchdogs
commands.description: Get/set service watchdog state
commands.documentation:
If no argument is given, print the current state of service runtime
watchdogs. If an optional boolean argument is provided, globally
enables or disables the service runtime watchdogs (WatchdogSec=) and
emergency actions (e.g. OnFailure=, StartLimitAction=). The hardware
watchdog is not affected by this setting.

commands.name: set-default
commands.description: Set the default target
commands.documentation:
Set the default target to boot into. This sets (symlinks) the
default.target alias to the given target unit.

commands.name: set-environment
commands.description: Set one or more environment variables
commands.documentation:
Set one or more systemd manager environment variables, as specified
on the command line. This command will fail if variable names and
values do not conform to the rules (ASCII letters, digits, underscore;
names cannot be empty or start with a digit).

commands.name: set-property
commands.description: Sets one or more properties of a unit
commands.documentation:
Set the specified unit properties at runtime where supported. This allows
changing configuration parameters such as resource control settings at
runtime. Many resource control settings (primarily those in
systemd.resource-control(5)) may be changed at runtime. Changes are
applied immediately and stored on disk for future boots unless
`--runtime` is passed. The syntax of the property assignment follows
closely the syntax of assignments in unit files. Multiple properties
can be set at the same time.

commands.name: show-environment
commands.description: Dump environment
commands.documentation:
Dump the systemd manager environment block. This is the environment
block that is passed to all processes the manager spawns. The output
is in the form "VARIABLE=value", suitable for sourcing into shells.
If special characters or whitespace are present, dollar-single-quote
escaping is used.

commands.name: show
commands.description: Show properties of one or more units/jobs or the manager
commands.documentation:
Show properties of one or more units, jobs, or the manager itself.
If no argument is specified, properties of the manager will be shown.
By default, empty properties are suppressed; use `--all` to show those
too. Use `--property=` to select specific properties. This command is
intended for computer-parsable output; use status for human-readable
output.

commands.name: sleep
commands.description: Put the system to sleep
commands.documentation:
Put the system to sleep. This delegates to the suspend, hibernate,
hybrid-sleep, or suspend-then-hibernate command depending on the
current configuration and state.

commands.name: soft-reboot
commands.description: Shut down and reboot userspace
commands.documentation:
Shut down and reboot userspace. Unlike reboot, this only restarts
userspace services and daemons while keeping the kernel running.
This is useful for faster reboots where hardware does not need to
be reinitialized. A new root file system can be set up on "/run/next-root/"
before invoking this command.

commands.name: start
commands.description: Start (activate) one or more units
commands.documentation:
Start (activate) one or more units specified on the command line.
Unit glob patterns expand to names of units currently in memory.
Note that units which are not active and are not in a failed state
are usually not in memory, and will not be matched by any pattern.
Use `--all` to also operate on inactive units referenced by other
loaded units.

commands.name: status
commands.description: Show runtime status of one or more units
commands.documentation:
Show runtime status information about one or more units followed by
most recent log data from the journal. If no positional arguments are
specified, shows the status of the whole system. Each positional argument
is treated as either a unit name, a glob pattern, or a PID to show the
unit containing that PID. This function is intended for human-readable
output; use show instead for computer-parsable output.

commands.name: stop
commands.description: Stop (deactivate) one or more units
commands.documentation:
Stop (deactivate) one or more units specified on the command line.
This command will fail if the unit does not exist or if stopping is
prohibited (see RefuseManualStop= in systemd.unit(5)). If a unit
that gets stopped can still be triggered by other units, a warning
containing the triggering units is shown. Use `--no-warn` to
suppress the warning.

commands.name: suspend-then-hibernate
commands.description: Suspend the system, wake after a period of
commands.documentation:
Suspend the system and hibernate after a period of delay if the
system remains suspended. The delay is determined by the system's
sleep configuration (see systemd-sleep(7)). If the system wakes from
suspend before the delay expires, it will not hibernate.

commands.name: suspend
commands.description: Suspend the system
commands.documentation:
Suspend the system. This will trigger a system suspend state where
system memory is kept powered on but most devices are powered off.
The system will resume from memory once woken.

commands.name: switch-root
commands.description: Change to a different root file system
commands.documentation:
Change to a different root file system. This is used during early boot
to switch from an initial RAM disk (initrd) to the actual root file system.
The SYSTEMD_IN_GLIBC_SHUTDOWN environment variable should be set during
this transition.

commands.name: thaw
commands.description: Resume execution of a frozen unit
commands.documentation:
Thaw (unfreeze) one or more frozen units. This is the inverse operation
to freeze and resumes the execution of processes in the unit's cgroup.

commands.name: try-reload-or-restart
commands.description: If active, reload one or more units, if supported, otherwise restart
commands.documentation:
Reload one or more units if they support it. If not, stop and then
start them instead. This does nothing if the units are not running.

commands.name: try-restart
commands.description: Restart one or more units if active
commands.documentation:
Stop and then start one or more units if the units are running. This
does nothing if units are not running.

commands.name: unmask
commands.description: Unmask one or more units
commands.documentation:
Unmask one or more unit files, undoing the effect of mask. This
command expects valid unit names only; it does not accept unit file
paths.

commands.name: unset-environment
commands.description: Unset one or more environment variables
commands.documentation:
Unset one or more systemd manager environment variables. If only a
variable name is specified, it will be removed regardless of its
value. If a variable and a value are specified, the variable is only
removed if it has the specified value.

commands.name: whoami
commands.description: Return unit caller or specified PIDs are part of
commands.documentation:
Return the units the processes referenced by the given PIDs belong to
(one per line). If no PID is specified, returns the unit the systemctl
command is invoked in.

tar.documentation: Store multiple files in a single archive. tar creates archives (commonly .tar or .tar.gz) that preserve file structure, permissions, and timestamps. Key operations: -c create, -x extract, -t list, -r append, -u update. Read from or write to files with -f; use - for stdin/stdout. Compress with -z (gzip), -j (bzip2), -J (xz). Preserve permissions with -p. Follow symlinks with -h. Exclude patterns with --exclude=PATTERN. List contents verbosely with -v. Extract specific files by specifying them after the archive name. Combine with gzip/bzip2/xz extensions automatically (filename.tar.gz). Use --strip-components to remove leading path elements when extracting.

tmux.documentation: Terminal multiplexer: run multiple sessions, windows, and panes in one terminal. tmux keeps sessions alive after disconnect. Key commands: tmux new -s name (create session), tmux attach (reconnect). Within tmux: Ctrl+b (prefix) then: c (new window), % (split vertical), " (split horizontal), d (detach), $ (rename). Navigate panes: arrow keys after prefix. Resize panes with Ctrl+b :resize. Scroll with Ctrl+b [ then arrow keys, q to quit. Send commands to panes: Ctrl+b :send-keys. Copy mode with Ctrl+b [. Sessions: tmux ls (list), tmux kill-session -t name. Config: ~/.tmux.conf. Chain commands: tmux new-session -d -s name. Share sessions: tmux attach -t name (multiple can attach).

Record with --run-time. Video filters with --video-filter. Audio effects with --audio-filter. Works on Linux, macOS, Windows, and mobile platforms.

Basic usage: watchexec -- npm run build. Ignore patterns with --ignore (gitignore-style). Debounce with --watch-when-idle or --debounce. Clear screen between runs with --clear. Restart processes with --restart. Signal handling with --signal (send SIGTERM before killing). Watch specific paths with --watch. Use --exts to filter by extension. Shell command with -s sh or -c. Stop on error with --stop-flag-error. Process group with --process-group. Environment variables control behavior (WATCHEXEC_*).

xargs.documentation: Build and execute commands from stdin input. xargs reads items from stdin (whitespace-delimited, or null-delimited with -0), and executes COMMAND once or more times with those items appended. Default COMMAND is echo. The command line is built until it reaches system limits; control size with -n (items per invocation) or -s (max chars). Run multiple invocations in parallel with -P N. Use -I {} to insert items at a placeholder in the command string. If any invocation exits 255, xargs stops immediately. When input contains spaces or newlines, use -0 with find -print0 for safe handling. Combine with --interactive (-p) to confirm each command.

zip.documentation: Package and compress files into a ZIP archive. zip creates archives compatible with PKZIP; unzip extracts them. Basic usage: zip archive.zip file1 file2 ... or zip -r archive.zip dir/. Add files recursively with -r; update existing archive with -u. Compression levels -1 (fastest) to -9 (smallest); default is 6. Encrypt with -e (prompts for password). Exclude patterns with -x; include only matching with -i. Remove original files after archiving with -m. Set archive comment with -z. Split archives with -s size. Use -@ to read file list from stdin. To extract: unzip archive.zip; list contents with -l. Archive automatically uses Zip64 for files over 4 GB.
